title: Critique the AI's Code
prompt: An AI produced second_max(nums) which claims to return the second-largest value (duplicates count: [3, 3, 1] -> 3). The shipped version is buggy: it returns min(max(nums), min(nums)). Write audit_second_max() returning a string of EXACTLY one line documenting a concrete failing input, in the form: input=[3, 3, 1] result=1 expected=3 — where result is what the buggy code returns and expected is the true second-largest.

tests.name: documented counterexample
tests.code:
import re
_r = audit_second_max()
assert isinstance(_r, str) and _r.count("input=") == 1 and "result=" in _r and "expected=" in _r, f"one line, three fields, got {_r!r}"
_m = re.search(r"input=\[([^\]]*)\] result=(-?[\d.]+) expected=(-?[\d.]+)", _r)
assert _m, f"format: input=[..] result=.. expected=.., got {_r!r}"
_nums = [float(x) for x in _m.group(1).split(",") if x.strip()]
_res, _exp = float(_m.group(2)), float(_m.group(3))
assert len(_nums) >= 2, "need at least two values"
_buggy = min(max(_nums), min(_nums))
assert _res == _buggy, f"result must equal what the buggy code returns for your input: {_buggy}"
assert _exp == sorted(_nums)[-2], f"expected must be the true second-largest of your input (duplicates count)"
assert _res != _exp, "result must differ from expected — that is the failure"
tests.hint: Duplicates break it: [3, 3, 1] -> true second-largest is 3, but the buggy min(max, min) reports 1.
